headline: ReadyTech deploying AI internally across software delivery to accelerate feature development and QA, and embedding AI into vertical products including local government and recruitment
reasoning: James Diamond explained that ReadyTech is benefiting from AI deployment on two fronts: internally within its software delivery team to produce more features, develop them faster, and QA them more rapidly; and externally by embedding AI capability into its vertical market products. Specific examples include a local government product that uses AI to help town planners work through large backlogs of development applications against planning requirements, and a recruitment product that helps organisations better find, match, and onboard talent. The company also has AI-driven features in its education segment.
quote: We're a software development company. I think there's two aspects of it for us. One is deploying the AI technology inside our own organization to be more efficient, to be more productive. That's going exceptionally well. You know, we've rolled it out across our software delivery team. We're able to produce more features to go into development. We're able to develop those features faster, we're able to QA them faster, and so we're able to get them in the hands of our customers faster, which is fantastic. We're also building our capability into our products, so we service a lot of different industry verticals. Local government would be a great example. And we know in local government there's an enormous backlog of development applications that need to be worked through. So that's a great opportunity for us to deploy AI capability in there that looks at the town planning requirements and looks at the development application, and helps the town planners work through that backlog in a more effective way.
episode_title: ReadyTech questions where the AI payoff is

headline: Enterprise AI spending is ramping rapidly with 1-in-5 organisations planning to invest $5-20 million in AI over the next 12 months, but ROI measurement requires a longer time horizon
reasoning: James Diamond noted that AI spending is accelerating significantly across the organisations ReadyTech surveyed, with 1 in 5 anticipating spending between $5 million and $20 million on AI over the next 12 months. However, he cautioned that the return on investment needs to be measured over a longer period because productivity gains tend to shift bottlenecks rather than eliminate them outright, and it is not until the entire value chain is unblocked that true returns in productivity and cost reduction emerge. He advised organisations to start using AI tools now but to do so with a security-first, privacy-first, and governance-first mindset, and to plan for returns over a longer term horizon.
quote: People are spending a lot. That's for sure. We're seeing organizations, you know, investing 5 to 20 million. 1 in 5 organizations that we polled anticipated spending that that range of investment in AI over the next 12 months. And the measuring of the ROI think's going to need to be done over a longer period of time. Often, often the productivity gains come, and then organizations have to grapple with what they do with that additional capacity. And in some cases, the first thing that happens is the bottleneck that's been unblocked, moves to another part of the business. They need to deploy AI technology there to unblock that bottleneck. And that process can take a couple of months to play out. And it's not until you unblock the entire value chain that you get the true return on investment coming through in terms of productivity, productivity uplift and maybe cost reduction as a function of that.
episode_title: ReadyTech questions where the AI payoff is
